questions.question: Distinguish magma from lava, name the three settings in which magma forms, and explain how silica content decides whether a volcano oozes or explodes.
questions.expected_answer: Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is the same material once it emerges. Both carry dissolved gases — mainly water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide — which power eruptions. Magma forms in three settings: at divergent boundaries, where separating plates relieve pressure on the mantle so rock melts by decompression; at convergent boundaries, where water sweated from the descending slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge above it; and at hot spots, where a plume of unusually hot mantle rises beneath the middle of a plate, as at Hawaii and Tristan da Cunha. Eruption style depends on viscosity, set mainly by silica. Low-silica basaltic magma is very hot, around 1 100 to 1 200 degrees Celsius, and runny, so gas escapes freely and eruptions are effusive — lava streams far and builds broad gentle slopes. High-silica andesitic or rhyolitic magma is cooler and stiff enough to seal its own vent, so trapped gas pressure builds for years until the seal fails and the eruption is explosive, ejecting pyroclastic ash, cinders and bombs. Volcanoes are classed as active, dormant or extinct.

questions.question: Explain the difference between extrusive and intrusive volcanic landforms, and show how both are written into the South African landscape.
questions.expected_answer: Extrusive landforms are built where magma reaches the surface: cones, craters, lava flows and lava plateaux, plus hot springs such as Badplaas and Goudini. South Africa's great extrusive feature is the Drakensberg-Lesotho lava plateau: about 180 million years ago, as Gondwana began breaking up, fissure eruptions flooded the interior with sheet upon sheet of basalt, and the surviving stack explains the escarpment's level ramparts and step-like skyline. Intrusive landforms crystallise underground and appear only after erosion strips their cover. A batholith is a vast deep granite body, exposed as rounded domes like the Cape Peninsula granites at Boulders Beach; a lopolith is a saucer-shaped intrusion, with the Bushveld Igneous Complex — the world's largest, holding the richest platinum and chromium reserves — as the example; a laccolith domes the overlying strata into a blister; a sill spreads between rock layers while a dyke cuts across them, both occurring throughout the Karoo as dolerite, where resistant sills cap the flat-topped koppies — most dramatically the columns of the Valley of Desolation near Graaff-Reinet — and dykes weather out as long straight ridges; and a volcanic neck or plug is magma frozen in the pipe, with the diamond-bearing kimberlite pipes at Cullinan and Venetia as South Africa's most valuable.

questions.question: Rank the main volcanic hazards, list the benefits that keep people living near volcanoes, and describe the management chain that saved lives at Mount Pinatubo in 1991.
questions.expected_answer: Lava flows destroy property but rarely kill, since most can be outwalked. The deadliest hazard is the pyroclastic flow, an avalanche of incandescent gas, ash and rock that outruns any vehicle — one destroyed St Pierre on Martinique in 1902 within minutes. Ash falls crush roofs, smother crops, foul water, damage lungs and ground aviation, as Eyjafjallajökull did across Europe in 2010. Lahars — ash mixed with rain or meltwater — bury valley towns far from the summit, as at Armero in Colombia in 1985. Further hazards include toxic gases, landslides, tsunamis and short-term global cooling after very large eruptions. People stay because weathered ash and lava give exceptionally fertile soils, as on Java and the slopes of Vesuvius; geothermal energy heats Iceland and drives Kenya's Olkaria power stations; mineral wealth concentrates in volcanic rocks, from Bushveld platinum to kimberlite diamonds; and volcanic landscapes draw tourists. Management works because volcanoes give warning: monitoring detects earthquake swarms, ground swelling, rising gas output and temperature, and converts them into alert levels; hazard maps mark lahar valleys and flow paths; planning keeps settlement out of the worst zones and rehearses evacuation. At Pinatubo in 1991 this chain — watch, map, plan, practise — evacuated tens of thousands before one of the century's largest eruptions.
